newsitem.title: UK: British inflation stubbornly above target.
newsitem.headline: British inflation stubbornly above target.

text.p: Britain's core rate of inflation stuck stubbornly at 3.1 percent in January, official data released Thursday showed, adding weight to the Bank of England's call for a rise in interest rates to keep price pressures in check.
The Office for National Statistics said core inflation, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, fell 0.2 percent in the month, but the annual rate was unchanged from December.
That left the inflation rate stubbornly above the government's target of 2.5 percent, which it originally aimed to hit before national elections due by May.
But the government insisted inflation would soon edge lower.

"Serious commentators, including the Bank of England in their Inflation Report yesterday, expect inflation to fall back over the coming months," Angela Knight, economic secretary to Britain's Treasury, said in a statement.
"The strength of sterling and this week's excellent producer price figures show inflation remains under firm control."
Headline annual inflation rose to 2.8 percent in January, its highest level in a year, from 2.5 percent in December.

Economists had expected core inflation to edge lower to 3.0 percent and the headline figure to edge up to 2.7 percent. They said the figures would help endorse the central bank's call for an immediate quarter point interest rate rise.
"This gives a little more credence to the Bank of England's view that we should see a small tightening in monetary policy in the near future," said Philip Uglow, an economist at Union plc.
The figures came a day after Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke dismissed the central bank's call for higher interest rates to keep price pressures under control.

Setting out its case in a key speech Tuesday and the quarterly inflation report Wednesday, the bank said rates needed to rise immediately by a quarter point to ensure the government hit its inflation target in the medium term.
If rates were left unchanged, inflation would pick up to around 3.0 percent or more within two years, the Bank said.
But Clarke said he had no intention of checking economic growth by raising the cost of borrowing.
"I think it is not yet at the stage where I have to put the brakes on," he said in a radio interview.
